As the Chinese Moon Festival approaches, I find myself in quiet reflection—no lantern to launch, no mooncakes to share, yet the same old hunger stirs within me. It is not for food, but for the memories that this festival always seems to revive. Years ago, when I was still small enough to be carried on my grandfather’s shoulders, we would make our way to the village river at dusk. The water shimmered like liquid silver, and above it the moon floated, luminous and ever-so-slightly golden. My grandfather would tell me stories of Chang’e, of the jade rabbit that pounds herbs with its pestle, of lonely lovers who find themselves united only in the light of the full moon. He did not speak of the astronomical mechanics behind eclipses or the dark side of the moon; he spoke of longing, of reunion, of the thin thread that links absent hearts across any distance.
